## Tensions and contradictions

1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.

2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.

3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.

4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.

5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.

6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]

7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.

8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.

9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.

10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

151	Once a training system is initiated, it should be constantly evaluated. The 
152	evaluation of the eﬃcacy of a training system can be undertaken in a 
153	multidimensional manner. The most simplistic assessments used to validate a 
154	training system are the actual performance improvements achieved in response to

156	measurements of physiological adaptation, such as hormonal or cell signaling

159	maximal anaerobic power, maximal aerobic power, maximal force generating

161	important role in this capacity, using their expertise to evaluate the athlete and

2.
 Determining the system’s structure
Once the factors central to the success of the training 
system are established, the actual training system can 
be constructed. A model for both short- and long-term 
training should be created. The system should be able 
to be applied by all coaches, but it should also be 
ﬂexible enough that coaches can enrich the system’s 
structure based upon their own experiences.

Third 
Principle
3.
 Validating the efﬁcacy or effects of the system
Once a training system is initiated, it should be constantly evaluated. The 
evaluation of the eﬃcacy of a training system can be undertaken in a 
multidimensional manner. The most simplistic assessments used to validate a 
training system are the actual performance improvements achieved in response to 
the system. More complex assessments can also be used, including direct 
measurements of physiological adaptation, such as hormonal or cell signaling 
adaptations. Additionally, mechanical assessments can be quantiﬁed to determine 
if the training structure is working eﬀectively; examples include the evaluation of 
maximal anaerobic power, maximal aerobic power, maximal force generating 
capacity, and peak rate of force development. Sport scientists can play a very 
important role in this capacity, using their expertise to evaluate the athlete and 
provide insight into how eﬀective a training system is. If the training system is not 
optimal, then the performance enhancement team can reevaluate and modify the 
system.

15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
17	each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
18	order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
19	appearance of an annual cycle in miniature" — a block resembling a preparatory period
20	(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
21	ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
22	a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
23	superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
24	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
25	months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
26	the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
27	effects" (unspecified in this chapter — likely developed in Chapter 3, not yet ingested).
28	The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
29	the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists five
30	claimed benefits of this design over the traditional model (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, and
31	Table 1.8, PDF p. 42, printed p. 31): reduced total training volume without reducing workout
32	count; more purposeful monitoring (fewer targeted abilities per stage); improved
33	psychological focus and motivation; more targeted nutrition per block (e.g., higher protein
34	during strength-focused blocks); and — most relevant to the peaking question — "a
35	multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
36	competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
37	season, not only at a single season-end date.
38	
39	**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
40	accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
41	is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
42	stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
43	Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
44	adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
45	superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks — the same
46	mechanism underlying [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].
47	
48	**When to apply** — This is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
49	miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
50	football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
51	this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
52	game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
53	relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
54	baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
55	football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
56	language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
57	"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
58	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21) — this Issurin framework offers a
59	more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
60	peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.
61	
62	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
63	figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check — Issurin gives no worked
64	example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
65	this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
66	multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage —
67	Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with
68	discrete competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing), and Chapter 3's
69	microcycle-level material (not yet ingested; see `_book.md` for the recommended next batch)
70	is likely necessary before this framework can be translated into a week-by-week in-season
71	football plan. **Contested — flag as unqualified:** the "does not work well for
72	high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative carries the same caveat as
73	in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] — Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already
74	in this library, is a current high-level training text that does not abandon
75	period-based (as opposed to stage-based) annual planning. **Inference:** Issurin's own 2016
76	review (Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached) is titled around benefits *and*
77	limitations of block periodization and likely qualifies the confident five-benefit list
78	above; this entry's claims should be revisited once that review is read.
79	
80	**Example** — A five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
81	accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
82	spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
83	Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
84	realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
85	Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).

# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks

**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
appearance of an annual cycle in miniature" — a block resembling a preparatory period
(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
effects" (unspecified in this chapter — likely developed in Chapter 3, not yet ingested).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists five
claimed benefits of this design over the traditional model (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, and
Table 1.8, PDF p. 42, printed p. 31): reduced total training volume without reducing workout
count; more purposeful monitoring (fewer targeted abilities per stage); improved
psychological focus and motivation; more targeted nutrition per block (e.g., higher protein
during strength-focused blocks); and — most relevant to the peaking question — "a
multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
season, not only at a single season-end date.

**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks — the same
mechanism underlying [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**When to apply** — This is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21) — this Issurin framework offers a
more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check — Issurin gives no worked
example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage —
Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with
discrete competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing), and Chapter 3's
microcycle-level material (not yet ingested; see `_book.md` for the recommended next batch)
is likely necessary before this framework can be translated into a week-by-week in-season
football plan. **Contested — flag as unqualified:** the "does not work well for
high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative carries the same caveat as
in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] — Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already
in this library, is a current high-level training text that does not abandon
period-based (as opposed to stage-based) annual planning. **Inference:** Issurin's own 2016
review (Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached) is titled around benefits *and*
limitations of block periodization and likely qualifies the confident five-benefit list
above; this entry's claims should be revisited once that review is read.

**Example** — A five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).

needing a multi-peak model), [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],

4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
5	book: block-periodization--issurin
6	chapter: "2.1.4, 2.2.2"
7	topic: key-workouts and key-exercises
8	category: [programming, workout-design, concentration]
9	confidence: supported

12	---
13	
14	# Key-Workouts and Key-Exercises Apply the Concentration Principle Inside a Single Session
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin extends the BPC concentration principle (see
17	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) down to the level of a single session.
18	A **key-workout** is the most important development session in a training cycle, focused on
19	the current main training emphasis (Table 2.5, PDF p. 56, printed p. 45): it targets the
20	cycle's most relevant abilities (usually one motor-fitness and one technique/tactics
21	target), demands focused athlete motivation and coach support, is timed for the athlete's
22	"best time" (adjusted to prior load but not overly fatigued), is loaded at a
23	substantial/large/extreme level, favors partnership/team-spirit organizational forms, and
24	requires thorough objective monitoring (chronometry, HR, blood lactate, video). New,
25	unfamiliar training means should *not* be introduced during a key-workout, since novelty
26	diverts attention and motivation from load-specific execution. Within a workout, the
27	analogous concept is the **key-exercise** (or **key-task** in team/combat sports where a
28	scrimmage or sparring session plays the role) — the single most important exercise, given
29	priority placement, maximal self-motivation and support, "prime-time" timing, and careful
30	monitoring (Table 2.9, PDF p. 64, printed p. 53). Issurin gives typical prescriptive ranges
31	for key-exercises by targeted ability (Table 2.10, PDF p. 67, printed p. 55, based on Fox &
32	Mathews 1981 and Viru 1995, "with author's modification"): maximal speed, 7-15s work at a
33	1:10 work/rest ratio, maximal intensity, 5-8 reps, 2-5 series; anaerobic glycolytic power,
34	30-50s, 1:(4-5), submaximal, 4-6 reps, 2-4 series, blood lactate >8 mmol/L and HR >180;
35	anaerobic glycolytic endurance, 1-1.5 min, 1:3, high intensity, 8-12 reps, 1-3 series,
36	maximal lactate >8 and HR >180; aerobic power, 1-2 min, 1:(1-0.5), intermediate, 5-8 reps,
37	1-3 series, lactate 4-8 and HR 160-180; aerobic endurance, 1-8 min, 1:0.3, medium intensity,
38	4-16 reps, 1-3 series, lactate 2.5-4(5) and HR 140-160; restoration/fat oxidation, 20-90 min,
39	low intensity, 1-3 reps, HR 100-140.
40	
41	**Why it works** — Concentrating mental focus, coach attention, and objective load-tracking
42	on one workout and one exercise per cycle (rather than treating every session as equally
43	important) is the same logic as the chapter-1 concentration principle applied at a smaller
44	time scale: it protects a genuinely high-value stimulus from being diluted or blunted by
45	surrounding fatigue and divided attention.
46	
47	**When to apply** — Programming a training cycle's hardest, most important session so it
48	actually gets the recovery state, attention, and monitoring it needs to produce the intended
49	adaptation, rather than treating every practice/lift as interchangeable. Table 2.10's
50	intervals give a concrete starting point for designing a key-exercise once the targeted
51	ability is chosen. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name an equivalent "key-workout"
52	concept explicitly, though the department's own metric-selection discipline (pick 1-2 output
53	metrics per force-plate report, per the Hawkin Dynamics ODSF framework,
54	`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring") reflects a similar
55	instinct toward concentrating monitoring attention rather than tracking everything equally.
56	
57	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own cautionary example (PDF p. 66, printed
58	p. 55) is that selecting the correct key-exercise is harder than it looks: at a national
59	coaching seminar of Olympic/World/Continental medalist-producing coaches, "more than 50%"
60	of proposed workouts confused exercises for maximal speed with exercises for speed endurance
61	(anaerobic glycolytic capacity), or aerobic endurance with aerobic power — i.e., experienced
62	coaches routinely mis-assign an exercise to the wrong physiological bucket. Table 2.10's
63	numeric ranges are themselves secondary citations (Fox & Mathews 1981; Viru 1995) filtered
64	through "author's modification" — the specific modification is not described, so treat the
65	exact numbers as Issurin's own adapted synthesis rather than a directly-reproduced published
66	table. This system also assumes a coach has the staff capacity for thorough, per-workout
67	objective monitoring (HR, blood lactate, video) — not always feasible outside individual/dual
68	sports with small rosters.
69

# Key-Workouts and Key-Exercises Apply the Concentration Principle Inside a Single Session

**What it is** — Issurin extends the BPC concentration principle (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) down to the level of a single session.
A **key-workout** is the most important development session in a training cycle, focused on
the current main training emphasis (Table 2.5, PDF p. 56, printed p. 45): it targets the
cycle's most relevant abilities (usually one motor-fitness and one technique/tactics
target), demands focused athlete motivation and coach support, is timed for the athlete's
"best time" (adjusted to prior load but not overly fatigued), is loaded at a
substantial/large/extreme level, favors partnership/team-spirit organizational forms, and
requires thorough objective monitoring (chronometry, HR, blood lactate, video). New,
unfamiliar training means should *not* be introduced during a key-workout, since novelty
diverts attention and motivation from load-specific execution. Within a workout, the
analogous concept is the **key-exercise** (or **key-task** in team/combat sports where a
scrimmage or sparring session plays the role) — the single most important exercise, given
priority placement, maximal self-motivation and support, "prime-time" timing, and careful
monitoring (Table 2.9, PDF p. 64, printed p. 53). Issurin gives typical prescriptive ranges
for key-exercises by targeted ability (Table 2.10, PDF p. 67, printed p. 55, based on Fox &
Mathews 1981 and Viru 1995, "with author's modification"): maximal speed, 7-15s work at a
1:10 work/rest ratio, maximal intensity, 5-8 reps, 2-5 series; anaerobic glycolytic power,
30-50s, 1:(4-5), submaximal, 4-6 reps, 2-4 series, blood lactate >8 mmol/L and HR >180;
anaerobic glycolytic endurance, 1-1.5 min, 1:3, high intensity, 8-12 reps, 1-3 series,
maximal lactate >8 and HR >180; aerobic power, 1-2 min, 1:(1-0.5), intermediate, 5-8 reps,
1-3 series, lactate 4-8 and HR 160-180; aerobic endurance, 1-8 min, 1:0.3, medium intensity,
4-16 reps, 1-3 series, lactate 2.5-4(5) and HR 140-160; restoration/fat oxidation, 20-90 min,
low intensity, 1-3 reps, HR 100-140.

**Why it works** — Concentrating mental focus, coach attention, and objective load-tracking
on one workout and one exercise per cycle (rather than treating every session as equally
important) is the same logic as the chapter-1 concentration principle applied at a smaller
time scale: it protects a genuinely high-value stimulus from being diluted or blunted by
surrounding fatigue and divided attention.

**When to apply** — Programming a training cycle's hardest, most important session so it
actually gets the recovery state, attention, and monitoring it needs to produce the intended
adaptation, rather than treating every practice/lift as interchangeable. Table 2.10's
intervals give a concrete starting point for designing a key-exercise once the targeted
ability is chosen. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name an equivalent "key-workout"
concept explicitly, though the department's own metric-selection discipline (pick 1-2 output
metrics per force-plate report, per the Hawkin Dynamics ODSF framework,
`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring") reflects a similar
instinct toward concentrating monitoring attention rather than tracking everything equally.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own cautionary example (PDF p. 66, printed
p. 55) is that selecting the correct key-exercise is harder than it looks: at a national
coaching seminar of Olympic/World/Continental medalist-producing coaches, "more than 50%"
of proposed workouts confused exercises for maximal speed with exercises for speed endurance
(anaerobic glycolytic capacity), or aerobic endurance with aerobic power — i.e., experienced
coaches routinely mis-assign an exercise to the wrong physiological bucket. Table 2.10's
numeric ranges are themselves secondary citations (Fox & Mathews 1981; Viru 1995) filtered
through "author's modification" — the specific modification is not described, so treat the
exact numbers as Issurin's own adapted synthesis rather than a directly-reproduced published
table. This system also assumes a coach has the staff capacity for thorough, per-workout
objective monitoring (HR, blood lactate, video) — not always feasible outside individual/dual
sports with small rosters.

**Example** — For a football skill player whose training cycle emphasizes maximal speed,
the key-exercise might be 6-8 reps of 7-15s maximal-intensity sprints at roughly a 1:10
work-rest ratio (per Table 2.10), placed early in the week's most-rested session, with
sprint times or GPS max-velocity data as the monitored variable — while other exercises in
that same session are deliberately treated as secondary, not co-equal priorities.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]].

15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
17	(Table 1.7, PDF p. 37, printed p. 26): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
18	endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
19	"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
20	endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
21	and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration — fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
22	targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
23	event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
24	going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
25	sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
26	realization. **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper (Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's
27	1.2.1 narrative (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22) use the term **transformation**; from section
28	1.2.2 onward (PDF p. 37+, printed p. 26+) and in the book's own tables, the term used is
29	**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
30	for either term should resolve to this entry.
31	
32	**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
33	abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
34	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
35	endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
36	residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
37	more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
38	superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
39	concurrent development of everything at once.
40	
41	**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
42	sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
43	together — see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
44	blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline** shows a structurally similar but
45	independently-arrived-at sequence: the department's own preparatory-period design goes
46	hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power
47	(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48) —
48	a general-to-specific progression that parallels accumulation-to-realization, though the
49	baseline's sequence is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect superimposition
50	logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.
51	
52	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
53	athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
54	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
55	carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
56	absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
57	clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Contested (partly):**
58	the vault's Bompa & Haff material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`)
59	independently describes a comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a
60	4-12 week delayed rebound — a longer and less rigidly three-staged model than Issurin's
61	roughly two-month training stage (below); the two should be read as convergent but not
62	identical prescriptions, and a program note should say which model's timing a given plan
63	follows.
64	
65	**Example** — A training stage built for a mid-season peak: 3-4 weeks of accumulation
66	(aerobic base, general strength), 3-4 weeks of transmutation (sport-specific conditioning,
67	strength-endurance, technique under fatigue), then 1-2 weeks of realization (tapered
68	volume, high-intensity model-speed work, full restoration) ending at the target competition
69	or test date.

14	# Bondarchuk's Own Four Exercise Classes, in His Own Words: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive
15	
16	**What it is** — This is the primary-source definition of the classification this book's
17	own title concept depends on, drawn from Bondarchuk's Glossary (not from Chapter 2's
18	prose, which assumes the reader already knows these terms):
19	- **General (Preparatory) Exercises / GPP**: "do not repeat the competitive actions as a
20	  whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part in the work being done. The
21	  functional systems of the body are activated but do not ensure an increase in results in
22	  the competitive exercise." Function: all-round development, work capacity, and active
23	  rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. x.)
24	- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the
25	  competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts. However, they use similar
26	  muscle groups in their execution," activating the functions and body systems the main
27	  movement depends on, with "identical or close to identical regimes of muscle work."
28	  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
29	- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises / SDE**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its
30	  separate parts. In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, together
31	  with activation of similar systems and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work
32	  regime and other systems of the body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry
33	  into the state of sports form." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
34	- **Competitive Exercises / CE**: "the acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the
35	  athlete participates in competition," executed either in actual competition or in
36	  training as a model/repeat of competitive conditions, easier or harder. (PDF p. 12,
37	  printed p. x-xi.)
38	Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
39	**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
40	jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
41	barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)
42	
43	**Why it works** — The four classes form an ordered continuum of how much of the
44	competitive movement (muscle groups, movement structure, muscle-work regime) an exercise
45	reproduces, which is the same logic underlying
46	[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
47	elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]: more shared
48	elements with the competitive movement should predict more reliable positive transfer.
49	Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) is this book's attempt to
50	test that prediction empirically, event by event.
51	
52	**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
53	selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
54	**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
55	preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
56	(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
57	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
58	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
59	gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
60	library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
61	`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
62	(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
63	entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
64	examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.
65	
66	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is Bondarchuk's own
67	classification scheme, widely adopted in the Soviet/Russian sport-science tradition and
68	cross-referenced by Verkhoshansky's circle (see the Related links), but it is a
69	practitioner taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
70	classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
71	sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
72	track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
73	single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
74	drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
75	addresses.
76	
77	**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
78	specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
79	different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot
80	(repeats the throw's parts under altered load); competitive = throwing the 7.26kg
81	competition shot in a meet.
82

# Evans's Own "Notable Giants" Lineage of Sport Science and Coaching

**What it is** - On a single slide titled "Notable Giants" (U1 L2 p.3), Evans lists thirteen
named people alongside a one- or two-word role tag, with no further elaboration on the slide
itself: Nicholai Bernstein (Motor Control), L.P. Matveyev (Sport Scientist / Coach), Yuri
Verkhoshansky (Sport Scientist / Coach, starred), Carmelo Bosco (Sport Scientist), Anatoliy
Bondarchuk (Coach), Henk Kraaijenhof (Coach), Atko Viru and Mehis Viru (Sport Scientist /
Coach, starred), Charlie Francis (Coach, starred), Michael Yessis (Professor / Coach,
starred), Tudor Bompa (Coach / Professor), Vladimir Issurin (Sport Scientist / Coach), Al
Vermeil (Coach), Johnny Parker (Coach), and Dan Pfaff (Coach). The slide does not explain
what the asterisks mean; a plausible reading is "authors Evans has read directly," but the
slide gives no legend, so this is Inference, not a stated fact. A separate slide in the same
lecture (U1 L2 p.5) names a "Sport Coach: Randy Huntington" under a low-resolution video
still, disconnected from the named-giants list, with no other text.

**Why it works** - The slide gives no mechanism or rationale for why this list, in this
order, constitutes "the" lineage; it functions as a syllabus of names to know rather than an
argued history. Inference: the list moves roughly from foundational Soviet motor-control and
periodization theory (Bernstein, Matveyev) through Soviet/Eastern-bloc training-methods
figures (Verkhoshansky, Bosco, Bondarchuk, the Virus) to Western popularizers and coaches
who studied or translated that material (Kraaijenhof, Francis, Yessis, Bompa, Issurin,
Vermeil, Parker, Pfaff), but this grouping logic is not stated on the slide itself.

**When to apply** - Useful as a checklist for which authors' names a student of this course
is expected to recognize before later lectures cite them (Bondarchuk, Verkhoshansky, Issurin,
and Bompa are each cited again by name and year in U3 L4-L5; see
[[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]] and
[[framework--issurin-microcycle-types-and-planning-steps]]). Eric's baseline names an
overlapping but not identical set as course-team influences (Vermeil, Bondarchuk, Verkhoshansky,
Zatsiorsky, Parker/Miller/Panariello, Prilepin, Fober; `method-baseline.md`, "Named
influences" table), which suggests convergence between the HHPR 5355 course material and
Evans's own course on which names matter, though the two lists are not identical (Evans
names Bernstein, Bosco, the Virus, Kraaijenhof, Yessis, Issurin, and Pfaff, none of which
appear in Eric's baseline's named-influences table; Eric's baseline names Zatsiorsky,
Panariello, Prilepin, and Fober, none of which appear on this Evans slide).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a bare name list with role tags, not a
substantive claim about any individual's ideas; treat it only as an index of who to expect
Evans to cite later, not as evidence for any specific training method. The slide gives no
sourcing for why these thirteen names and not others, so completeness cannot be assessed.
Confidence is untested: this is one slide from a practitioner course, uncorroborated by any
other source in this library.

**Example** - When Evans later cites "Bondarchuk" for a 3-principle training-system model
(U2 L4, see [[framework--bondarchuk-three-principles-of-training-system-construction]]) or
"Bompa, 2009" for annual-plan structure (U3 L4-L5), this slide is the place those names were
first introduced in the course, unglossed.

**Related** - [[framework--bondarchuk-three-principles-of-training-system-construction]],
[[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]],
[[framework--issurin-microcycle-types-and-planning-steps]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion:
`supertraining--verkhoshansky/_book.md` and `transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/_book.md`
could each note that this course-lecture entry independently lists their authors among a
lineage of "giants," as a light corroboration of those authors' standing in the field
(not of any specific claim).

# Anokhin's Functional System: Central Nervous, Neuromuscular, and Energy-Supplying Subsystems Gathered Into One

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U1 L3 p.10) credits "P. Anokhin" with a model in which the
"Human Organism" and "Its physiological systems" (Central nervous system, Neuromuscular
system, Energy-supplying system) are "Activated & Gathered into" a "FUNCTIONAL SYSTEM." The
next slide (p.12) states each subsystem's specific job in this functional system: the Central
nervous system's role is "Increasing capacity to produce the necessary intensity of impulses
from the central motor area to the periphery and to ensure appropriate intra and
inter-muscular coordination"; the Neuromuscular system's role is "Improving the function of
the motor apparatus in accordance with the work regime"; the Energy-supplying system's role
is "Enhancement of the energy providing sources and setting up the marriage between them."
The slide gives no citation year or source text for Anokhin's model.

**Why it works** - The slide gives no mechanism for how these three subsystems are
"activated and gathered" into a single functional system beyond naming Anokhin as the
originator; it presents the three-part division and each part's stated role as given facts,
not as something derived from data shown on the slide. Inference: this framing appears
designed to argue that improving "power output" (the topic of the surrounding slides, see
[[framework--power-output-as-final-goal-of-competition-exercise]]) requires improving all
three subsystems together, not any one in isolation, since the model calls them a single
integrated system rather than three independent parts.

**When to apply** - As a three-part checklist (CNS, neuromuscular, energy-supply) when asking
whether a given training intervention is actually addressing the system that limits a
specific athlete's performance, rather than assuming any one subsystem (e.g., "more
strength") is always the answer. Eric's baseline does not name Anokhin or this specific
three-subsystem model; the closest baseline parallel is the department's own emphasis on
athlete monitoring across multiple systems rather than a single test
(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment").

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The slide does not explain what would count as evidence
that a subsystem has been "improved," nor does it give any worked example applying this
three-part model to a specific athlete or sport within this lecture. Confidence is untested:
this is a single unelaborated slide citing one named author (Anokhin) with no year, no
original text quoted, and no corroboration elsewhere in this course or library.

**Example** - Not given on the slide; Evans does not walk through a worked example of the
functional-system model in this lecture.

**Related** - [[framework--power-output-as-final-goal-of-competition-exercise]] (same
lecture, same "how do you improve power output" thread).

# Increasing Power Output Is the Final Goal of Training for Competition Exercise

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U1 L3 p.6) quotes Yuri Verkhoshansky, 2011, directly: "May
almost always be related to the capacity to express power produced by the speed of movements
and by the force of overcoming external resistance," and "Consequently, the training process,
focused on improving the sports result, represents the process of increasing the POWER
OUTPUT of competition exercise." The following slides define power mathematically (Work per
unit time, Watts; Power = Force x Velocity, p.7) and give two "factors in increasing power
output": a biomechanical perspective ("Human movement is an interaction between the human
body and the external environment (Bernstein)," p.8) and a physiological perspective ("Human
movement represents an interaction between the human organism and the external environment
(Verkhoshanksy)," p.9, sic on the spelling). The book does not give the original publication
this 2011 quote is drawn from.

**Why it works** - The quoted passage states power output as the training objective but does
not itself explain the physiological mechanism by which force x velocity training raises
competitive power output; the slide's "biomechanical" and "physiological perspective" bullets
restate the interaction-with-environment framing rather than supplying a causal chain.
Inference: linking this claim to the later "Two Factors to Increase Sport Result" slide (p.14,
see [[framework--two-factors-special-work-capacity-technical-mastery]]) suggests Evans's
intended chain is: competitive result depends on power output, power output depends on
force x velocity capacity specific to the sport (special work capacity) plus the skill to
apply it (technical mastery) - but this chain is Inference, built by the entry writer across
two slides, not stated as a single argument by Evans himself.

**When to apply** - As a framing question when evaluating any strength or power program:
does this exercise or method plausibly raise the force x velocity output specific to the
competitive movement, or is it improving something else (e.g., general work capacity,
hypertrophy) that may or may not transfer? Eric's baseline does not use this exact
Verkhoshansky quote, but its programming philosophy independently emphasizes exercise
selection along a general-to-competitive spectrum and matching training to the "amplitude/
direction of movement... dynamics of effort... rate/timing of force production" (`method
-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing the Principle of Dynamic Correspondence,
Verkhoshansky), which is consistent with (though not identical to) this power-output framing.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The slide gives no numeric example of measuring "power
output of competition exercise" for any actual sport skill, and no citation locator (book
title, page) for the 2011 Verkhoshansky quote beyond the year. Do not treat "power output" as
a single measurable variable without specifying which movement and which units; the
comparison later in the same lecture between a "sprinter" and a "marathoner" (p.13) implies
the relevant power-output value is sport-specific, but the slide gives no numbers for either.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The lecture's only example is qualitative: a "SPRINTER vs. MARATHONER" power
output comparison slide (p.13) with no numbers, framed as "these changes are dependent on...
the demands of the sport."

**Related** - [[framework--anokhin-functional-system-three-subsystems]],
[[framework--two-factors-special-work-capacity-technical-mastery]].

# Issurin's Five Domains of the Training Process: Physical, Technical, Tactical, Psychological, Intellectual

**What it is** - Evans's slide "The Training Process" (U1 L3 p.15, repeated verbatim as
"Training Domains" at U2 L4 p.4), cited to "(Issurin, 2008)," gives a five-row table of
Domain and Purpose: Physical, "To improve physical (motor) abilities and increase the
physiological potential of athletes"; Technical, "To acquire cognitive technical skills and
attain the desired level of technical mastery"; Tactical, "To acquire cognitive sport-specific
tactics, which allow for the most effective utilization of athlete's motor and technical
abilities in competition"; Psychological, "To develop the athlete's personality so that it is
harmonious, highly motivated and morally stable. To instill the skills of cognitive
self-regulation of the athlete's emotional state in order to facilitate maximum realization of
their psycho-physiological potential"; Intellectual, "To improve athletes' general and
sport-specific knowledge in order to effectively complete their training and competitive
program." No book title or page number is given beyond the year.

**Why it works** - The slide states the five domains and each one's stated purpose as given
categories; it does not explain why training is best divided into exactly these five domains
rather than some other number, nor does it cite empirical support for the division.
Inference: the table's function in this course is taxonomic, providing vocabulary the
lecturer uses later, for example the "Training Process" slide in U4 L1 p.4 which lists the
same five domains and then explicitly narrows the coach's own scope ("Tactical: Limited to
zero influence. Technical: Limited to zero influence") to argue why a strength coach's
monitoring effort should concentrate on the Physical, Psychological, and Intellectual
domains.

**When to apply** - As a checklist when scoping what "training" a role is actually
responsible for; Evans's own later use of this table (U4 L1 p.4) is to argue that a strength
and conditioning coach has real influence over three of the five domains and should not
overreach into Tactical or Technical. Eric's baseline's four departmental operating
principles (Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance,
Performance Team Collaboration, Research and Development) are a different taxonomy for a
different purpose (departmental scope, not training-domain scope) and do not map one-to-one
onto Issurin's five domains, though both are attempts to bound a role's responsibility
(`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles").

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a secondary citation (Evans citing Issurin) with
no book title, edition, or page given; the entry writer has not independently verified this
table against Issurin's original text (Issurin's "Block Periodization" book is separately
staged in this library at `block-periodization--issurin`, but its ingest map does not yet
show this exact five-domain table among its atomized chapters 1-2 entries as of this
ingest). Treat the wording above as Evans's slide transcription, not a verified quotation of
Issurin. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - Evans's own applied example is in U4 L1 p.4: he assigns himself (as strength
coach) an active role in Physical ("Build bigger, more efficient engines"), Psychological
("Pocket psychologist, surrogate parent, cheerleader"), and Intellectual ("Mentor and
educator of the training process... Influence them to be their own manager") domains, while
explicitly disclaiming Tactical and Technical influence.

**Related** - [[framework--two-factors-special-work-capacity-technical-mastery]],
[[framework--adime-monitoring-process]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion: if
`block-periodization--issurin` later atomizes a matching five-domain table from Issurin's own
text, link back here to confirm or correct this secondary citation.

# Evans's Own Caveat: the Fitness-Fatigue Model Is "Just a Concept," Not an Empirically Validated Model

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U1 L5 p.3-4) introduces the Fitness-Fatigue Model ("Fatigue
can mask fitness") and then immediately qualifies it: "Theoretical Model, only useful if you
provide evidence. Marathon running... 400m runner? Strength, speed, jumping, aerobic
capacity, etc... No empirical evidence to put a model together with all the biomotor
qualities together. JUST A CONCEPT" (capitalization as on the slide). He does not cite a
specific paper making this critique; it reads as his own assessment, offered in his own
lecturing voice.

**Why it works** - This is Evans's own critical framing, not a claim he attributes to another
author; he does not explain in this slide what evidentiary standard would satisfy him (what a

# Homeostasis Holds a Setpoint Constant; Allostasis Changes the Setpoint to Meet Anticipated Demand

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U1 L4 p.17-22) present two distinct regulatory models. He
credits "1935 - Walter Cannon" with Homeostasis: "Processes in the organism to preserve
constant conditions within which are centered around specific set points and governed by
negative feedback loops" (p.15). He credits "Sterling & Sayer in 1988" (the slide's spelling;
the well-known 1988 paper is by Sterling and Eyer) and "Jay Schulkin" with Allostasis: "Process
by which an organism achieves internal viability through a bodily change of state," further
distinguishing "Allostatic State" ("Chronic OVER-ACTIVATION of regulatory systems and the
alterations of body set points") from "Allostatic Overload" ("expression of pathophysiology
by the chronic over-activation of regulating systems") (p.17). A direct-comparison slide
(p.19) credited to "Bruce McEwen" states: "Homeostasis describes mechanisms that HOLD
CONSTANT a controlled variable by sensing its deviation from a 'setpoint' and feeding back to
correct the error. Allostasis describes mechanisms that CHANGE a controlled variable by
predicting what level will be needed and overriding local feedback to meet anticipated
demand." The worked example given is blood pressure: "120/80 is 'normal.' What happens if it
jumps up to 150/100?" with the answer, credited to "(Sterling, Eyer, 1998)" on the following
slide (note: this citation year, 1998, differs from the 1988 year given two slides earlier for
the same Sterling and Eyer source; the slide deck does not reconcile this discrepancy, so both
years are recorded here as they appear): "Brain sets blood pressure via multiple, mutually
reinforcing mechanisms. Negative feedback mechanisms are acutely overridden. When demand
persists, all mechanisms are reset to operate at the new level."

**Why it works** - The slides state the distinction (fixed setpoint with feedback correction,
versus a setpoint that shifts to anticipate demand) but do not explain the underlying neural
or endocrine mechanism connecting a training stimulus to a shifted setpoint beyond the blood
pressure example; that example itself only asserts "the brain sets blood pressure via multiple
mechanisms" without detailing what those mechanisms are. Inference: applied to training
adaptation, the distinction implies that some training-induced changes (e.g., a durably raised
resting heart rate range under chronic overreaching) may be better modeled as an allostatic
setpoint shift than as homeostatic disturbance-and-recovery, but Evans does not make this
application explicit in this lecture; it is a plausible follow-on question left open by his
own subsequent slides on Verkhoshansky's training-load-to-allostatic-overload model
(U1 L4 p.26-33), which are not atomized as a separate entry in this ingest because they
closely resemble already-staged Supertraining content on supercompensation and adaptive
reconstruction (see Related below).

**When to apply** - As a vocabulary distinction when discussing whether an athlete's altered
baseline (elevated resting HR, altered HRV baseline, elevated resting blood pressure) under
sustained hard training reflects a genuine allostatic setpoint shift versus ordinary
homeostatic strain that will resolve with recovery. Eric's baseline discusses HRV-adjacent and
readiness-monitoring concepts without using homeostasis/allostasis vocabulary specifically
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," "Recovery and sleep"), so
this framework offers language not currently present in the baseline, though its practical
application to Baylor's monitoring stack is not demonstrated by Evans in this lecture.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The citation years for Sterling and Eyer are internally
inconsistent on Evans's own slides (1988 on p.17, 1998 on p.22); this entry records both as
written rather than silently picking one. The blood pressure example is illustrative, not a
worked case with real data; no actual athlete or training example is given anywhere in this
segment of the lecture. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The blood pressure "120/80 to 150/100" illustration described above is the
lecture's only worked example, and it is hypothetical, not a real measured case.

**Related** - Reciprocal-link suggestion:
`supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation.md` and
`supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--strength-training-threshold-stimulus.md` cover
Verkhoshansky's training-load-to-adaptation model, which Evans's own next slides (U1 L4
p.26-33, citing "Verkhoshansky, 2012") apply the allostasis/allostatic-overload vocabulary to
directly; a reviewer with both books staged should check whether Evans's 2012-cited version
adds or conflicts with anything in those two Supertraining entries before atomizing it
separately.

# Morphobiomechanics: A Seven-Type Constitutional Body Classification

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U2 L3 p.20) credits "Dorohov, RN and Guba, VP from Smolensk
State Academy of Physical Education, Sport and Tourism, Division of Anatomy and Biomechanics"
with a "morphobiomechanics" system naming seven constitutional body types: Mesosomatic (MeS),
Microsomatic (MiS), Macrosomatic (MaS), Megalosomatic (MegS), Nanosomatic (NanS),
Micromesosomatic (MiMeS), and Mesomacrosomatic (MeMaS). The slide states the system is
"Designed to differentiate different human body constitutional types (anthropometry, muscle
mass structure, bone structure, body fat mass)" but gives no definition of what distinguishes
any one of the seven types from another, no cutoff values, and no citation year or source
publication.

**Why it works** - The slide names the concept without elaboration, per the source's own
sparse-slide format; it gives no criteria for classifying an athlete into one of the seven
types, so no mechanism can be extracted beyond the stated purpose (differentiating body
constitution across anthropometry, muscle mass, bone structure, and body fat).

**When to apply** - Not currently applicable in practice from this lecture alone; the slide
does not provide enough information to classify an athlete or interpret what training
implications follow from a given type. It is recorded here as a named framework Evans
introduced, should the CVASPS transcript or another source later supply working definitions
of each of the seven types. Eric's baseline does not reference this classification system or
any equivalent constitutional-type framework; its anthropometric material focuses on
Performance Nutrition-owned body composition tracking, capped at four times per year
(`method-baseline.md`, "Nutrition and body composition"), which is a different measurement
purpose (composition tracking over time, not constitutional-type classification).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This entry cannot be used to classify a real athlete: no
definitions, thresholds, or worked examples are given anywhere in this lecture for any of the
seven type names. Do not infer body types from name etymology alone (e.g., assuming
"Macrosomatic" means simply "large body") without a primary source, since the slide gives no
such definitions. Confidence is untested, and this is one of the clearest cases in this
course of "the slide names a concept without elaboration," per the task brief's rule for this
source.

**Example** - Not given anywhere in this lecture.

matches "morphobiomechanics," "somatotype," or any of the seven type names (checked by grep
across both).

# Evans's Worked Example: Applying the Five Dynamic-Correspondence Criteria to a Wrestling Clinch Takedown

**What it is** - After presenting the standard five Dynamic Correspondence criteria
(amplitude/direction of movement, accentuated region of force production, dynamics of effort,
rate and time of maximum force production, regime of muscular work - the same five-factor list
Eric's baseline independently records as course material, `method-baseline.md`, "Strength and
power," citing the Principle of Dynamic Correspondence, Verkhoshansky), Evans's slides (U2 L4
p.21-22) work through a specific technique: "Takedown from a clinch that is executed from the
position of having low double under hooks secured against the lower back of the opponent."
His analysis, quoted directly: amplitude/direction - "Lifting the opponent begins in an
upward rotational fashion that allows the hips to transition for the downward rotational
movement during the throw towards the mat... The amplitude of hip and back extension is
rather small as the lift is initiated from a relatively upright posture to begin with while
the subsequent rotational element is more pronounced"; region of force production - "The
point in which the greatest forces are generated is when the hips and back are nearly fully
extended as you take balance away from your opponent by lifting him or her partially or
completely off the mat"; dynamics of effort and rate/time of force production - "the
lift/throw is where the greatest speed is generated and the time of execution may be
quantified, albeit in a rudimentary fashion, via a coach with a stop watch who estimates the
distance over which the movement is performed... arrives at a workable figure for rate and
time"; regime of muscular work - the initial hip control to immobilize the opponent is "an
isometric, or sustaining, muscle effort," while the subsequent throw "consists of dynamic
(moving) and ballistic (explosive) muscle effort."

**Why it works** - Evans does not state a mechanism for why walking through these five
criteria on a specific technique improves exercise selection beyond the general Dynamic
Correspondence premise (shared movement amplitude, force region, effort dynamics, force
timing, and muscular-work regime should predict better transfer, a premise this course does
not re-derive but assumes from the earlier slides). Inference: the value of this example is
methodological, not mechanistic - it demonstrates how a coach without laboratory equipment can
still apply the five criteria qualitatively (his own phrase, "albeit in a rudimentary
fashion... via a coach with a stop watch") to a single competitive technique, rather than only
to whole sports in the abstract.

**When to apply** - As a template for walking a coach through the same five-question audit on
any single competitive skill (a football block, a tackle, a route break) when selecting
weight-room exercises intended to transfer to it. Eric's baseline notes that HHPR 5355 teaches
this same five-factor Dynamic Correspondence model in the abstract but does not record a
worked single-technique example in the transcript material reviewed for the baseline
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power"); this Evans example fills that specific gap with
a concrete, if combat-sport-specific, illustration of the method.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a single illustrative example on a wrestling
technique, not a validated case study with measured data; Evans supplies no actual timing,
force, or EMG data for this takedown, only a qualitative walk-through, and he explicitly
concedes the timing method he describes ("void of accounting precisely for the curvilinear
pattern") is approximate. Do not treat this as evidence that the five-criteria method
produces accurate or reliable exercise-selection decisions; it demonstrates the method's
steps, not its validity. It is also sport-specific to wrestling's clinch takedown; applying
the same five questions to a different sport's skill (e.g., a football pass-rush move) would
require a new, separate qualitative analysis, not a direct transfer of this one's conclusions.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The wrestling clinch takedown itself, described above, is the example.

Verkhoshansky's own statement of the Dynamic Correspondence criteria (the entry writer did

should compare that entry's dimension count and wording against the five-factor version used
here and in Eric's baseline, and link them if they describe the same underlying model at
different levels of detail.

# Three Types of Overload: Stimulating, Retaining, Detraining

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U2 L4 p.15) names "3 Types of Overload": (1) Stimulating -
"Magnitude of the training load is above the neutral level - heightened adaptation"; (2)
Retaining - "Magnitude is in the neutral zone - maintained preparedness"; (3) Detraining -
"Magnitude of the training load leads to a decrease in performance, the functional
capabilities of the athlete, or both." No author or citation is given for this specific
three-way naming on this slide, though it appears in the same lecture segment as other
Bondarchuk- and Issurin-cited material.

**Why it works** - The slide defines each overload type by its outcome (heightened
adaptation, maintained preparedness, or decreased performance) relative to an unnamed
"neutral level," but does not state how to measure or identify that neutral level for a given
athlete; no mechanism is given for why loads above versus at versus below that level produce
these three different outcomes, beyond the general adaptation-stimulus logic given on the
preceding slide (U2 L4 p.14: "Increasing stimulus -> adaptation -> performance improvement...
Lack of stimulus -> plateau... Excessive stimulus -> maladaptation -> decrease in
performance").

**When to apply** - As a three-way classification for describing the intent of a given
training block or phase: is this phase meant to stimulate new adaptation, retain current
fitness during a competing priority (e.g., in-season), or is a planned detraining/deload
period. This maps onto Eric's baseline's in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`), which functions as a Retaining-type overload
strategy in this framework's terms, though the baseline material does not use this specific
three-way vocabulary.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The slide gives no numeric or percentage definition of the
"neutral level" that separates Stimulating from Retaining from Detraining loads for any
specific biomotor quality or athlete population; without that, this framework is a labeling
scheme for outcomes observed after the fact, not a prospective dosing tool. No citation is
given, so its origin (Bondarchuk, Issurin, or Evans's own synthesis of the surrounding cited
material) cannot be confirmed from this slide alone. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No worked example with specific loads or athletes is given in this lecture.

**Related** - [[framework--three-types-of-overload-stimulating-retaining-detraining]] shares
its underlying stimulus-to-outcome logic with the "3 Basic Scenarios" slide on the same page
(U2 L4 p.14) and with the "Undertraining / Overreaching / Overtraining" continuum slide (U2
L4 p.16), which uses a four-way version (Undertraining, Overreaching, Overtraining, plus
Acute overload) of essentially the same underlying dose-response idea; see also
[[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]] (U3 L1) for Evans's later, more detailed
overtraining-specific version of this same underlying dose-response logic.

# "Intensity Will Define the Biological Target. Volume Is How Deep You Want to Go."

**What it is** - Evans's closing slide on Training Load (U2 L6 p.20), titled "Intensity &
Volume...", states in his own words: "Intensity will define the biological target." "Volume
is how deep you want to go." This follows earlier slides in the same lecture defining
Intensity as "a function of neuromuscular activation (NA)," with NA pattern "dictated by the
external load, the speed of performance, the amount of fatigue accrued, and the type of
exercise undertaken" and noting a psychological dimension ("Something can have LOW strain yet
high psychological strain," p.15), and Volume as "time or duration of training... the
distance covered or the volume load in RT (volume = reps x sets x resistance)... Volume for
different biomotor qualities need to be compared amongst themselves. You cannot compare
mobility volume to maximal strength volume" (p.13).

**Why it works** - The slide does not explain the physiological mechanism connecting a given
intensity level to a specific "biological target" (e.g., which intensity range targets which
energy system or fiber type is not stated on this slide, though it is addressed elsewhere in
the course, e.g. the energy-system power/capacity tables in U2 L1); this is offered as a
compact planning heuristic, not a mechanism claim. Inference: read alongside the volume
definition's caveat that different biomotor qualities' volumes are not directly comparable,
the heuristic's practical implication is that a coach should first fix the intensity (which
determines what quality is being trained) before deciding how much volume (how much of that
specific quality) to prescribe, rather than planning volume and intensity independently.

**When to apply** - As a quick planning check when writing a training block: has the
intensity been set first, to establish which biological quality is actually being targeted,
before volume is added within that target? Eric's baseline does not use this specific phrase,
but its Prilepin's-chart-based approach to daily rep/set assignment by percentage of 1RM
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19`) operates on a structurally similar premise: pick
the intensity zone (percentage of 1RM) first, then assign volume (reps and sets) within it.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a compact aphorism, not a quantified model; it
gives no specific intensity thresholds or their associated "biological targets," so it cannot
be applied mechanically without the more detailed content elsewhere in the course (e.g., the
energy-system power/capacity time bands in U2 L1, or Prilepin-style percentage zones, neither
of which this specific slide references directly). Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific numeric example is given on this slide.

**Related** - None found elsewhere in this library under this specific phrasing.

# The Overtraining Continuum: Acute Fatigue, Functional and Non-Functional Overreaching, Overtraining

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U3 L1 p.10), titled "Overtraining Continuum," presents a
four-stage progression by increasing training/fatigue and decreasing outcome, with no
individual citation given on this specific slide (the surrounding lecture cites no author by
name for this table): Acute Fatigue (timescale: day(s); outcome: increase in performance);
Overreaching, Functional (FOR) (timescale: days/weeks; outcome: temporary decrease, then
recovery); Overreaching, Nonfunctional (NFOR) (timescale: weeks/months; outcome: decrease or
no change, recovery takes weeks to months); Overtraining (timescale: months to a year+;
outcome: decrease, recovery takes months to a year or more). Functional Overreaching is
further defined (p.12): "Stimulates physiological adaptations, which compensate for
training-related stress. Recovery can take days to weeks depending on the stimulus
magnitude." Nonfunctional Overreaching (p.13): "Occurs when intensified training is continued
and results in the stagnation or decreases in performance that would require longer recovery
times. When NFOR is continued for a long period of time, the athlete will eventually reach a
state of overtraining." Overtraining (p.14): "a process of excessive training & non-training
stressors in high performance athletes that may lead to persistent fatigue, performance
decrements, neuroendocrine changes, alterations in mood states, and frequent illness," most
notably upper-respiratory-tract infections, with "Overtraining Syndrome" defined as "a
neuroendocrine disorder that may result from the process of overtraining."

**Why it works** - The slide states the stages and their approximate timescales and outcomes
but does not give the diagnostic criteria for distinguishing one stage from the next in real
time (e.g., what specific performance drop or duration marks the transition from FOR to
NFOR); Evans's own later slide in the same lecture (p.17, see
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]) states directly that "a
definitive diagnostic tool for OTS is not available," which is consistent with this
continuum being a retrospective classification (assigned after recovery time is observed)
rather than a prospective diagnostic test.

**When to apply** - As shared vocabulary for describing where an athlete's underperformance
likely sits on a severity/duration spectrum, and for setting expectations about recovery
timescales at each stage. Eric's baseline does not use this specific FOR/NFOR/OTS
terminology; its closest material is the department's mRSI-based daily readiness monitoring,
adopted specifically to catch problems early via objective daily testing rather than through
symptom-based staging (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"
citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`) - a different (earlier-warning, objective) approach
to the same underlying underperformance-and-recovery problem this continuum describes.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No citation is given for this specific four-stage table
on this slide, so its exact source (a specific consensus statement or review) cannot be
verified from this lecture alone. The timescales given (days, days/weeks, weeks/months,
months-to-a-year+) are stated as general ranges, not derived from a specific study or athlete
population; do not treat them as precise thresholds for any individual athlete. Confidence is
untested.

**Example** - No specific athlete case is given; the table is presented generically.

**Related** - [[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]],
[[principle--recovery-is-a-training-means]],
[[framework--three-types-of-overload-stimulating-retaining-detraining]] (U2 L4, an earlier and
coarser three-way version of the same underlying dose-response logic).

# "Recovery Is Not Simply a Thing. It Is a Part of a Logically Sequenced Training Plan. Recovery Is a Training Means."

**What it is** - Evans states, in his own words (U3 L1 p.6): "Recovery is not simply a
'thing'. It is a part of a logically sequenced training plan. Recovery is a training means."
This follows a slide on "Preparedness" (p.5) stating: "The best way to increase an athlete's
preparedness is to induce restoration and adaptation by implementing a properly designed
periodized training program that uses logical variations in volume, intensity, and exercise
selection. By including appropriate variation in the training regime, the athlete will have
periods of reduced training volume, reduced training intensity, and complete rest, all of

training-related stress. Recovery can take days to weeks depending on the stimulus

times. When NFOR is continued for a long period of time, the athlete will eventually reach a
state of overtraining." Overtraining (p.14): "a process of excessive training & non-training

decrements, neuroendocrine changes, alterations in mood states, and frequent illness," most
